ORIGINAL USMLE-STYLE PRACTICE

Sternoclavicular injury: 1

After shoulder trauma, a patient has a prominent medial clavicular end projecting forward at the sternoclavicular joint. There is localized pain without dysphagia or respiratory compromise. Which displacement direction best matches the palpable deformity?

  1. Urgent reduction with appropriate specialist support
  2. Anterior medial-clavicle displacement
  3. Posterior medial-clavicle displacement
  4. Medial clavicular physeal injury
  5. CT assessment of the SC region
Answer and explanation

Anterior medial-clavicle displacement

Anterior SC dislocation commonly produces a palpable prominence over the joint.

Option explanations

Anterior medial-clavicle displacement: Anterior SC dislocation commonly produces a palpable prominence over the joint.

Posterior medial-clavicle displacement: Posterior displacement can compress the trachea, esophagus and major vessels. This does not best answer the specific question in this case.

Medial clavicular physeal injury: The late-closing medial clavicular physis can mimic SC dislocation in young patients. This does not best answer the specific question in this case.

CT assessment of the SC region: Plain radiographs can be difficult to interpret; CT defines SC displacement and adjacent anatomy. This does not best answer the specific question in this case.

Urgent reduction with appropriate specialist support: Posterior SC dislocation requires a controlled setting because manipulation can endanger adjacent major vessels. This does not best answer the specific question in this case.
